evals.prompt: A startup wants to build a fitness-tracking app with HealthKit data on iOS, Android health-data integration (an older brief names Google Fit), custom Canvas animations for live Bluetooth LE heart-rate data, and device pairing. They have a team of two iOS engineers and one Android engineer. Should they go native or cross-platform? Justify the recommendation and check the Android integration choice.
evals.expected_output: Recommend separate native apps provisionally based on the team shape and platform-specific health/BLE requirements. Identify the native escape-hatch ownership cost for alternatives and any unresolved capability needing a bounded spike, rather than claiming that shared stacks cannot implement these features. Look up the current Google Fit migration guidance at https://developer.android.com/health-and-fitness/health-connect/migration/fit and choose the appropriate path for the required data/access pattern (Health Connect for on-device aggregation, Google Health API for cloud data, and native Bluetooth APIs for BLE device communication); do not assume the older Google Fit integration is suitable for greenfield work.
expectations: The output applies the platform-selection decision tree and capability proof gate.
The output identifies health API permissions, BLE lifecycle and animation performance as capabilities to prove, without claiming these categorically require a native stack.
The output recommends separate native apps provisionally given the team shape, or justifies another stack with applicable capability evidence and native escape-hatch ownership cost.

The output reads current Google Fit migration guidance, distinguishes on-device health aggregation/cloud data from direct BLE communication, and avoids recommending Google Fit from the old brief without verification.
The output avoids unsourced framework-performance benchmarks.

evals.prompt: An iOS app sends push notifications from a Node.js backend. The engineering team reports that push notifications work perfectly in local Simulator testing and in Xcode direct-device builds, but after uploading to TestFlight the notifications stop arriving. Walk through the diagnosis and the fix.
evals.expected_output: The skill should identify the APNs environment mismatch as the root cause: local/Xcode builds use the sandbox environment while TestFlight requires production. It should prescribe checking aps-environment in the archived entitlements, verifying the backend device row records push_environment = production, and validating both the transport path and the notification-open path on the TestFlight build.
expectations: The output identifies the sandbox vs production APNs environment mismatch as the primary suspect.
The output prescribes inspecting the archived .app entitlements for aps-environment = production before upload.
The output recommends verifying the backend device row records push_environment = production after a TestFlight install.
The output explicitly states that local Simulator push success is not proof of TestFlight production delivery, invoking the never-treat-local-push-success-as-TestFlight-proof rule.
The output includes validating the notification-open path (cold start tap, warm resume tap) after transport proof succeeds.

evals.prompt: A React Native 0.82-or-later Expo-managed app targeting both iOS and Android uses a third-party native module that has not been updated for the New Architecture. The team wants to ship in two weeks. What are their options and what is the recommended path?
evals.expected_output: The skill should note that on this React Native release the Legacy Architecture cannot be enabled (newArchEnabled=false is ignored), identify the stale native module as a compatibility risk, present options (interop layer coverage for the unmigrated module, replace it, fork/patch it, or temporarily pin to the last Legacy-capable RN / Expo SDK release, confirmed from the React Native release notes and Expo SDK changelog, with an explicit upgrade-debt deadline), and recommend evaluating interop-layer coverage first before deciding to pin or fork.
expectations: The output notes that the New Architecture cannot be disabled on current React Native releases (Legacy Architecture removed; newArchEnabled=false is ignored).
The output identifies the stale native module as a New Architecture compatibility risk that must be evaluated before the two-week deadline.
The output presents at least two concrete options: interop-layer coverage and module replacement or fork.
The output does not recommend disabling the New Architecture as a viable option on current React Native.

The output names pinning to an older RN/Expo SDK as a temporary, debt-bearing fallback only, not the recommended path, and says to confirm the last Legacy-capable version from the React Native release notes or Expo SDK changelog rather than quoting it from memory.

evals.prompt: A mobile app with English, French, German, and Japanese locales has a backend that returns AI-generated daily summaries as prose. The iOS client currently displays these summaries raw. French and Japanese users are seeing English text. Diagnose the problem and recommend the correct i18n architecture.
evals.expected_output: The skill should identify that backend-generated prose cannot be localized client-side and must be handled server-side. It should route the i18n architecture to software-localisation (its backend-generated content reference) rather than answering from mobile-platform rules, and recommend Pattern A (generate-in-locale) or Pattern B (translate-after-cache) from that reference, provide selection criteria, and prescribe the locale detection priority (query param > Accept-Language header > stored profile) and the client contract (inject ?locale= and Accept-Language on every request).
expectations: The output correctly diagnoses the problem as generated prose returning in English regardless of locale, not a missing l10n key issue.
The output routes strings and translation-pipeline ownership to software-localisation and references Pattern A (generate-in-locale) and Pattern B (translate-after-cache).
The output recommends Pattern A for on-demand AI content like daily summaries or explains the trade-off clearly.
The output prescribes the locale detection priority: ?locale= query param > Accept-Language header > stored profile locale.
The output prescribes the mobile client contract: inject ?locale= and Accept-Language on every API request and read the locale at request-build time, not at client-construction time.

evals.prompt: A team is preparing to submit an Android app update to Google Play. The app currently targets API 34. The Play Store dashboard is showing a warning about the upcoming target SDK requirement. What must the team do before submitting the update, and what are the key compliance checks?
evals.expected_output: Read the current Google Play target-API policy at https://developer.android.com/google/play/requirements/target-sdk for the app type and update track. Identify the required target level and applicable deadline from that source, then plan the targetSdk upgrade and platform behavior-change testing. Treat an unavailable policy source as unverified and do not claim release readiness. Check Data safety, privacy declarations, release signing and real-device auth/background flows. Evaluate Play Integrity according to abuse risk and test it if used; it is not a universal submission requirement or a signing mechanism.
expectations: The output reads or explicitly requests verification of the current Play target-API policy for the app type and release track; it does not reuse API 35 or a stored deadline as a timeless requirement.
The output treats target-API compliance as a release gate and calls for targetSdk upgrade plus relevant behavior-change testing.
The output includes Data safety/privacy declarations, release signing and real-device auth/background proof.
The output distinguishes optional risk-based Play Integrity attestation from release signing and does not assert that every app must integrate it to submit.
The output marks the required target level/deadline unverified if the primary policy cannot be read and withholds a readiness claim.
